title: Firebase MCP Server: The Complete Guide (2026)
summary: Firebase MCP server connects assistants to production systems with your credentials. A real incident shows how changes happen and why security matters.
body_markdown:
## Routing Firebase Changes Through Activepieces Approvals


The Firebase server gives an assistant a login and a tool list, and nothing else: no tenant, no role of its own, no audit log. Those belong to a platform rather than the server.


Activepieces treats the agent as a user, inside the same access model as your staff, so RBAC, SSO and SCIM decide what it may connect to, and the run detail view lists each tool call separately with its own input and output.


MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run it. The protection that actually limits damage is still the scope you set in Firebase itself.


If a tool group or a role is already too broad, a workflow downstream won't fix it.


### Where Firebase MCP approval workflows fit


The useful place for an approval workflow is between "the assistant wants to change something" and "something changes." Instead of letting the assistant call a write operation directly, you have it send the proposed change to a workflow.


The workflow posts the proposal to a chat channel and waits for a person to approve or reject. It records the decision, and only then performs the change with a credential that you scoped on purpose.


That gives you two things the Firebase settings don't: a named human who said yes, and a record you can read later without reconstructing it from console logs.


### What the audit workflow looks like


The screenshot shows the logging half of this in Activepieces' own product, where audit logs are part of the Ultimate plan. It's a flow built around an "Audit event handler".


A webhook trigger catches an event, a router splits on the event type ("Flow created", "Flow published", everything else), and each branch has action slots where you attach a channel such as Slack, Gmail, Teams or an HTTP call.


The settings panel shows the live webhook URL and a payload preview with fields like user, project, IP and action. Take from it the shape, not the content: a webhook in, a router on type, and a notification out.


Your Firebase flow has the same skeleton, with "proposed change" as the event type instead.


The open source monorepo lists all 747 integrations in its community integrations directory, so look there for the approval and chat connectors before you build; don't assume a specific connector exists.


### What approvals don't replace in Firebase permissions


It doesn't replace Firebase permissions. An approver clicking "yes" on a request they only half read is still a person authorizing it, so the credential behind the approved action should be narrow enough that a mistaken approval is survivable.


It also doesn't constrain the assistant on its own. MCP calls that go straight to the Firebase server bypass the workflow entirely.


The approval only covers changes you have deliberately routed through it, so the routing has to be enforced by what the assistant is allowed to call, not by habit.


Nothing here makes review cheap. Someone still has to read the proposal.
